title: Anchor messaging heuristics for LLM endpoints
body:
Purpose
This is a lightweight, rep-facing heuristics sheet for anchoring messaging vs generic LLM API competitors. Focus: fast qualification, high-signal demo hooks, compact rebuttals, and traps to exploit for customers worried about cost, reliability, and private deployments. Not comprehensive — use this as a live playbook during sprint coaching.

Elevator (30s)
We help engineering teams run LLMs in production with predictable latency, lower per-token costs, and simple control over reliability and privacy. Unlike public LLM endpoints that trade off observability or force a single hosting model, Redwood gives teams the same API surface across hosted, reserved, and private deployments so you scale without rewriting integration or sacrificing SLAs.

Top 6 messaging anchors (priority order)
1) Predictable economics (anchor: unit-cost + commitment flexibility)
- Primary point: Customers pay for units with clear batch/cache levers; reserved pools let you guarantee throughput and unit pricing for heavy inference workloads.
- Quick rep line: "If you need to control your per-response cost, Redwood gives programmatic levers (batching, cache, quantization profiles) and reserved capacity options that avoid surprise bills."

2) Unified API across environments (anchor: no-rewrite migration)
- Primary point: Same SDK and routing config for hosted, dedicated, and private — simplifies compliance migrations and A/B rollouts.
- Demo hook: Switch model routing from hosted to private in the console and show the same tokens/response shape.

3) Reliability + graceful degradation (anchor: model fallbacks & routing policies)
- Primary point: Built-in model fallback, regional routing, and capacity tiers keep critical paths online even during cloud or model outages.
- Trap to exploit: Ask about their incident where a third-party model slowed down; highlight our canary + automatic fallback policies.

4) Observability & cost attribution (anchor: token-level telemetry)
- Primary point: Per-route and per-token metrics enable engineering and finance to attribute cost to features or routes.
- Rebuttal when competitor claims parity: "They may expose latency metrics, but do they expose token-level cost per route + KB of KV cache hits?"

5) Private deployments & compliance (anchor: VPC/HSM + audit trail)
- Primary point: Private control plane + KMS/HSM integrations and optional on-prem package for regulated data.
- Qualification question: Do you have data residency or audit log mandates?

6) Quality-first rollout tooling (anchor: evals + regression alerts)
- Primary point: Continuous evals, prompt set regression alerts, and canary policies reduce production regressions after model changes.

Competitor blindspots and traps (short list)
- Single-mode hosting: Many LLM APIs optimize for simplicity but force you into their hosted model; ask about migration time.
- Black-box economics: Some vendors surface token counts but not batching/cache levers — anchor cost conversation to unit economics, not just headline price.
- Limited fallbacks: If competitor lacks automatic model fallback, they require manual intervention during outages.
- Poor tracing: Few alternatives let you tie model outputs back to request routes, prompts, or fine-grained metrics.

Objection ladder + scripts (fast):
- Objection: "We already use [competitor]." -> Reply: "Totally fine — where do you see pain? If it's cost or outages, we can run a short eval side-by-side on your busiest routes and show unit economics and latency under production traffic."
- Objection: "Your API is more complex." -> Reply: "We keep the surface small — the extra knobs (batching, cache profiles, reserved capacity) are optional but pay back quickly for production traffic. We can show a 5-min setup that uses defaults, then a follow-up where you tune for cost after baseline."
- Objection: "We can't move off our vendor due to contracts." -> Reply: "We commonly start with non-critical routes (embeddings, QA tier) and prove cost/latency wins; then customers expand. Also note our private mode fits many compliance constraints that public vendors can't meet."

Qualification checklist (questions to prioritize in discovery)
- SLOs: target P95/P99 latency?
- Traffic shape: bursty or steady? token distributions? peak sequence length?
- Economics: how do you currently measure $/response or $/minute CPU? Any surprise bills recently?
- Compliance: data residency, HSM/KMS, audit log needs?
- Operational: available on-call bandwidth; tolerance for manual intervention on model regressions?
- Migration pain: how many teams/pipelines will need to change client code?

Demo playbook (3-minute sequence)
1) Quick context (30s): state customer's two biggest constraints (e.g., latency and cost).
2) Console switch (45s): show same API route switching from hosted->dedicated and note no code changes.
3) Metrics drill (45s): open route-level dashboard, show token-level cost breakdown and a simulated cache hit improvement.
4) Fallback test (30s): trigger a model failover policy and show automatic fallback in logs/traces.
5) CTA (30s): propose a one-week pilot with 2 critical routes and metrics baseline.

Win criteria for pilot/handoff to AE
- Clear baseline: P95 latency and $/1000 responses before Redwood pilot.
- Demonstrated improvements: >=10% unit cost reduction or improved P95 under same throughput.
- Operational sign-off: infra/security ok with routing and private options.

Signals of risk (early)
- Procurement block: long lead-time vendor contracts without pilot carve-out.
- Team bandwidth: no one available to collaborate on instrumentation or baselining.
- Unclear telemetry: customer cannot produce baseline token counts or route breakdowns.

Collateral to drop (quick list)
- Hosted vs Dedicated one-pager (tailored to infra leads)
- Pilot cheat-sheet: checklist + expected data points
- Short demo video: switching routing + fallback

Tactical notes to reps (internal)
- Always anchor to a measurable unit (tokens, latency SLOs).
- Use the fallback story early with reliability-concerned buyers — it's an emotional win.
- If competitor touts cheapest headline price, ask for sample monthly usage and simulate batching/cache to reveal true cost.
- Log every instance of competitor failing to provide route-level telemetry — we’ll use these anecdotes in field plays.

Open questions / follow-ups
- Need a short comparative table (our knobs vs top3 competitors) — ask product for a 1-pager. (Owner: Liam)
- Create two 90s demo recordings: 1 infra-focused (latency/cost) and 1 security-focused (private deploy). (Owner: Sara)

Notes-to-self (work-in-progress)
- Consider adding a one-sentence customer-facing test scenario: "We will run your top-2 routes through our pilot under production-like traffic for 7 days."
- Capture 3 recent field anecdotes where fallback saved a deal (for storytelling).

End.
